content: 1. Prolongation of the QT interval and isolated cases of torsades de pointes have been reported with certain second-line tuberculosis (TB) medications. These drugs should not be used in patients with known QT prolongation, hypokalaemia, or in combination with other drugs that prolong the QT interval. 2. The addition of isoniazid to treatment regimens has not shown clear evidence of either benefit or harm. However, for patient convenience, fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) of isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide (HREZ) may be used alongside levofloxacin for Hr-TB treatment. 3. High-dose isoniazid (10–15 mg/kg/day in adults) was not evaluated in this review due to insufficient data. However, in vitro evidence suggests that increasing the dose of isoniazid may be effective in cases with specific inhA mutations (and no katG mutations). In such cases, a maximum dose of up to 15 mg/kg/day could be considered. 4. Levofloxacin may interfere with lamivudine clearance, potentially increasing lamivudine levels, but it is not contraindicated with other antiretroviral agents, and no dose adjustments are required. However, co-administration with oral divalent cation-containing compounds (e.g., antacids) should be avoided as they impair levofloxacin absorption. Restriction of milk product consumption is unnecessary. 5. Extending treatment beyond six months may be considered for patients with extensive cavitary disease or those slow to convert to negative smear/culture. In such cases, resistance to rifampicin, fluoroquinolones, and pyrazinamide must be ruled out. These patients require careful monitoring and follow-up. 6. Cost-effectiveness analysis was not performed for this review. However, the use of FDCs, even partially, reduces costs. Medicines for a 6HREZ-levofloxacin regimen cost approximately three times more than a 2HREZ/4HR regimen when using the HREZ FDC. The treatment of Hr-TB according to these guidelines is not expected to significantly increase operational costs. 7. In settings where only the 3-drug FDC (HRZ) is available, ethambutol must be administered separately. The presence of isolated katG or inhA mutations corresponds to variable minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) levels, and their presence does not always indicate lowor high-level isoniazid resistance. However, the presence of both mutations usually indicates high-level resistance. 8. Regimens containing levofloxacin (750–1000 mg/day), moxifloxacin (400 mg/day), or gatifloxacin (400 mg/day) were included in studies. Early-generation fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin) are no longer recommended for drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) treatment. Gatifloxacin is unavailable in quality-assured formulations. 9. WHO guidelines recommend that all patients with TB strains resistant to rifampicin be placed on an MDR-TB treatment regimen. The addition of high-dose isoniazid and/or ethambutol may strengthen the regimen. 10. Longer MDR-TB regimens, typically lasting 20 months or more, are designed to maximize relapse-free cure rates while minimizing toxicity. These regimens may be standardized or individualized based on patient needs. The composition of these regimens is guided by the selection of effective medicines and the need to combine sufficient agents to ensure efficacy. 11. WHO recommends including levofloxacin or moxifloxacin in longer MDR-TB regimens. Bedaquiline should also be included for patients aged 18 years or older. Linezolid is strongly recommended for inclusion in longer MDR-TB regimens. 12. Clofazimine and cycloserine (or terizidone) may be included in longer MDR-TB regimens. Ethambutol and pyrazinamide may also be included, but their use is conditionally recommended with very low certainty in the evidence. 13. Amikacin may be included in longer MDR-TB regimens for patients aged 18 years or older if susceptibility is demonstrated and adverse reactions can be adequately monitored. If amikacin is unavailable, streptomycin may replace it under the same conditions. 14. Ethionamide or prothionamide may only be included in longer MDR-TB regimens if better options (e.g., bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, or delamanid) are unavailable. Similarly, p-aminosalicylic acid may only be included under these conditions. 15. Imipenem-cilastatin and meropenem should be administered with clavulanic acid, which is only available in formulations combined with amoxicillin. Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is not considered an additional effective TB agent and should not be used without imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem. 16. Longer MDR-TB regimens with sufficient effective agents are associated with higher cure rates and lower mortality in adults and children. The evidence base for many MDR-TB medicines relies heavily on observational studies, with few randomized controlled trials available. As a result, the overall certainty in the evidence is often graded as low or very low. 17. Monitoring and evaluation of patients on the (H)REZ-levofloxacin regimen should include clinical and laboratory testing. Signs of non-response or treatment failure should prompt drug susceptibility testing (DST) for rifampicin resistance and, if possible, for fluoroquinolones and pyrazinamide. 18. Monthly monitoring of liver function tests is essential for all patients receiving this regimen, particularly those at high risk (e.g., co-infected with viral hepatitis or with a history of heavy alcohol use). Early signs of ethambutol toxicity, such as retrobulbar neuritis, should be monitored, especially in pediatric populations. 19. WHO guidelines recommend that longer MDR-TB regimens include at least five effective medicines during the intensive phase. If only one or two Group A agents are used, both Group B agents should be included. If necessary, Group C agents may be added to complete the regimen. 20. The inclusion of newer medicines like bedaquiline and delamanid, along with reductions in the prices of moxifloxacin and linezolid, has made these regimens more accessible. Longer regimens are now being reviewed to optimize their composition and duration based on updated evidence.
